question: The two circles intersect at two points P and Q. PR and PS are diameters of the two circles. What is ∠PQR ?
solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

According to the circle theorem, the angle subtended by a diameter at any point on the circumference is always a right angle.

Here, PR is given as the diameter of the first circle.

Since the circles intersect at P and Q, point Q lies exactly on the circumference of the first circle.

Therefore, the angle subtended by the diameter PR at point Q must be exactly 90º.

**∴ The correct answer is 90º.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

**Given:**

⇒ Two circles intersecting at points P and Q.

⇒ PR is the diameter of the first circle.

⇒ PS is the diameter of the second circle.

**Concept Used:**

⇒ Angle in a semicircle is exactly 90º.

**Calculation:**

⇒ For the first circle, PR acts as the primary diameter passing through the center C1.

⇒ According to fundamental circle properties, any given diameter subtends an angle of exactly 90º at any arbitrary point on the circumference.

⇒ Since point Q lies on the exact circumference of the first circle, ∠PQR = 90º.

⇒ Similarly, looking at the second circle, PS acts as the diameter passing through C2.

⇒ Since Q also naturally lies on the circumference of the second circle, ∠PQS = 90º.

⇒ We can observe that adding these angles gives ∠PQR + ∠PQS = 90º + 90º = 180º.

⇒ This logically confirms that points R, Q, and S uniformly lie on a single straight line, but the question strictly asks for ∠PQR.

⇒ Hence, the angle ∠PQR evaluates to 90º.

**∴ The correct answer is 90º.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

Angle in a Semicircle

An angle inscribed in a semicircle (subtended by a diameter) is universally a right angle (90º). This happens because the central angle of a straight line is 180º, and any inscribed angle is exactly half of its central angle.

Collinearity in Intersecting Circles

When two distinct diameters starting from a common primary intersection point of two intersecting circles are drawn, their other endpoints and the secondary intersection point are always collinear, forming a completely straight line of 180º.

Cyclic Quadrilateral

If a generic quadrilateral is purely inscribed within a defined circle (all four vertices touching the circumference), the sum of its opposing interior angles structurally remains exactly 180º.
